What insights have you gained from this experience that you might carry into the future?

(I look up, my expression is earnest and a little haunted.)

My first instinct was to start pacing, to grab my phone. But then I remembered the card. My hand was actually shaking when I took it out of my purse. And honestly? The words... "this is not a new storm"... they just felt like a lie. They felt completely ridiculous while my heart was hammering.

But I did what we said. I didn't try to believe it. I just held it. Felt the corners. And I... I stood in the middle of the kitchen and just pushed my feet down into the linoleum. It felt so stupid. But I just did it. The storm was still raging... but maybe... maybe one tiny part of me was just feeling the floor instead. And holding a card.

Counselor: It sounds like you faced a really challenging moment with a lot of intensity, and yet you found a way to ground yourself amidst that storm. I appreciate your honesty about how the words on the card felt in the moment, and it’s powerful that you chose to focus on the physical sensations of your surroundings. How do you think that small act of grounding yourself contributed to your ability to manage the emotions during that time? What insights do you have about your coping strategies moving forward?

(I look down at my hands again, tracing the memory. The difference is so subtle, it's hard to put into words. I take a slow breath.)

Usually... after the panic subsides and Lars walks in the door, safe... there's this awful second wave. It's shame. It's this hot, horrible feeling that I'm completely broken, that I failed again. I can barely look at him because I feel so guilty for having imagined him... you know.

(I look up, and there's a fragile sense of wonder in my expression.)

This time... when he came in, I was just... relieved. The shame was still there, but it was like a whisper instead of a roar. Because... I realized my job wasn't to stop the panic. My job was just to hold the card and feel my feet. And... I did that. I didn't fail.

Later that night, I actually wrote it down, like we talked about. The ship's log. I just wrote, "7:15pm. Hurricane was an 8. But the floor was still there." And seeing it... it wasn't a record of me failing. It was just... a record of me surviving. It changed the story of what happened.

Counselor: It’s really inspiring to hear how you navigated that moment and how you reframed your experience in the ship's log. I... I'm not sure what it means. Honestly, it just felt like I was following the instructions we came up with in here. It felt like *your* voice in my head, telling me what to do.

(I look up, and my expression is filled with a kind of earnest confusion. I'm not trying to be difficult, I genuinely believe this.)

But... I was the one who wrote it down. It was my handwriting. That part was real. So I guess... I guess it means maybe the light from your flashlight lasts for a little while after I leave the room. I just don't know for how long.

Counselor: It’s completely understandable to feel uncertain about the implications of this shift in perspective; it’s a significant realization. You mentioned that writing it down in your own handwriting felt real, which suggests that you have the ability to carry this insight with you. (I look down, my hands twisting in my lap again. The praise feels nice, but fragile, and the question about what to do next feels like a huge responsibility I'm not ready for. My stomach gives a small, anxious flutter.)

I... I'm not sure. My head immediately goes back to what you said last week. About... our sessions ending.

(I look up, my expression is worried and earnest.)

I'm so afraid that Tuesday was just a fluke. A lucky break. I just keep thinking, what happens if a real storm hits? Like a 10 out of 10. I'm worried that my little card and my feet on the floor just won't be enough. It feels like I need... a bigger boat, maybe? Before I'm ready to sail by myself. I don't know what that means, but... that's how it feels.

Counselor: It’s completely valid to feel apprehensive about the future and to question whether your coping skills will hold up during more intense storms. I guess... I guess it tells me that building the boat will take a very long time. Plank by plank.

(I look up, my expression is filled with a deep, certain kind of dread. The fragile hope is gone.)

But what does it matter how big the boat is? The ocean is just... it's everything. It feels like I'm just building this little boat, working so hard on it, just so it can be swallowed by some monster wave that comes out of nowhere. I just know that's what will happen. Counselor: It sounds like you're feeling a heavy sense of dread and inevitability about the future storms you might face, and that's completely understandable given the intensity of your emotions. But it doesn't *feel* like a warning from a crew member. It feels like the truth. It feels like he's the only one who's looking at the same dark sky I am, while everyone else is pretending it's a sunny day. It doesn't sound like one person's opinion. It sounds like the roar of the ocean itself.

But... that doesn't prove the watchman is a liar. It just proves he was wrong *that time*. Don't you see? His job is to be wrong a hundred times, a thousand times, to protect me from the one time he's right. So when I look at the log... I just see that we got lucky on Tuesday. Counselor: It sounds like you're grappling with a lot of uncertainty and the weight of the watchman's voice, which can feel very convincing. (I look up, my expression is weary but searching. I'm trying to hold onto the new ideas, the ones that feel so flimsy.)

But... based on what we've been saying... maybe that's not it. Maybe the captain's job isn't to stop the wave. Maybe her job is just... to hold the wheel as steady as she can. And... and to take down the sails so they don't rip. And to tell the crew to hang on.

It's not about avoiding the wave. It's just about... getting through it. Without the whole ship breaking into a million pieces. That's... a very different job. A much smaller one.

Counselor: It sounds like you're beginning to redefine what it means to be a captain in your own life, shifting from the idea of avoiding all storms to one of navigating through them with resilience. I... I don't know. A small thing...

Maybe... you know, in the evenings, after the kids are asleep and the house is quiet? That's when the watchman sometimes starts his patrol. The... the 'what if something happens tomorrow' thoughts. Usually I just pace, or I get stuck looking at my phone, reading things I shouldn't.

(I look up, my expression is uncertain, as if I'm asking for permission.)

Maybe... taking down the sails would be... just making their school lunches for the next morning. Even if I feel the panic starting. (I search your face, needing to know if I'm on the right track.)

Is that... is that the kind of thing you mean?

Counselor: It sounds like you've identified a meaningful and practical way to take a small step towards preparing for the next day, even in the face of the watchman's thoughts. Yes. That feels... doable. It doesn't ask me to be brave or to fight anything. It just asks me to make a sandwich.

I'm still scared the watchman will be screaming so loud that I can't even open the refrigerator. But... this doesn't feel like an argument with him. It just feels like... a job. Yes. I can try to do that job.

Counselor: It sounds like you've found a tangible and manageable way to anchor yourself amidst the noise of the watchman's warnings, which is a really important realization. You too. See you next week.

See you next week.
